content: Iron(II) sulfate, also known as ferrous sulfate or copperas, is a chemical compound with the formula FeSO₄. It is most commonly encountered as the blue-green heptahydrate form. Iron(II) sulfate exists in various hydrated states, several of which occur naturally. These include: FeSO₄·H₂O (mineral: szomolnokite) FeSO₄·4H₂O FeSO₄·5H₂O (mineral: siderotil) FeSO₄·7H₂O (mineral: melanterite) When heated to 90°C, the heptahydrate form loses water and converts into the colorless monohydrate, which is also referred to as green vitriol or copperas. In the steel finishing process, prior to plating or coating, steel sheets or rods are treated in sulfuric acid pickling baths. This process generates large quantities of iron(II) sulfate as a byproduct. Commercially, iron(II) sulfate is also produced by oxidizing pyrite or by reacting iron with sulfuric acid. Ferrous sulfate is widely used in water purification processes, particularly for flocculation and phosphate removal in municipal and industrial sewage treatment plants. This helps prevent eutrophication in surface water bodies. Additionally, it is employed as a reducing agent, primarily for reducing chromate in cement. In the field of nutrition, ferrous sulfate is used to treat iron-deficiency anemia. Common side effects of this therapy include nausea and epigastric discomfort, which can be mitigated by taking the supplement at bedtime. Historically, during the 18th and 19th centuries, copperas was indiscriminately administered by untrained individuals to enslaved people for various ailments. Its known ability to induce severe nausea and vomiting made it a widely used remedy, often leading to poisoning and death. Today, ferrous sulfate is also used to fortify foods with iron, such as enriched cornmeal in products like Cheetos. In coloring applications, ferrous sulfate is a key ingredient in the production of inks, particularly iron gall ink, which was extensively used from the Middle Ages until the American Revolution. It is also used as a mordant in wool dyeing. In the 18th century, a method known as china blue was developed in England for applying indigo dye using ferrous sulfate. This process involved reducing indigo to leuco-indigo in baths of ferrous sulfate, followed by reoxidation to indigo in air. While this method allowed for sharp designs, it could not produce the deep hues achieved by other techniques. Ferrous sulfate is also used to stain concrete with a yellowish rust color and to give maple wood a silvery hue in woodworking. In horticulture, ferrous sulfate serves as a lawn conditioner and moss killer. During the latter half of the 19th century, it was also used as a photographic developer for collodion process images. Additionally, ferrous sulfate is sometimes added to the cooling water in brass turbine condenser tubes, where it forms a protective, erosion-resistant coating on the inner surfaces of the tubes.
